figures.title: Module map
figures.why: the module is one argument — Coulomb's law summed three ways — and the map shows which block sums it how.
figures.data: the structure of Parts 0–14: the force law, the three bookkeepings (field, flux, potential), what each is best at, and where the Olympiad layer attaches.
figures.read: The map groups the chapter around one Coulomb law and three equivalent bookkeeping tools: force, field/flux and potential.

figures.title: The element-and-symmetry method
figures.why: seven derivations in this chapter are the same five moves; seeing them as one flow is what makes the rod, the disc and the arc feel like one problem.
figures.data: the five steps of §3.4 and the two exits — a symmetry axis exists (integrate one component) or it does not (integrate two components, or switch to the potential of §3.29).
figures.read: Follow the symmetry branch: keep one axis component when symmetry cancels the rest; otherwise integrate vector components or switch to potential.

figures.title: Axial field of a charged ring
figures.why: the curve is the first non-monotonic field in the chapter, and its maximum at $x=R/\sqrt2$ is a standard question.
figures.data: $E_x/(kQ/R^2)=(x/R)/\bigl(1+(x/R)^2\bigr)^{3/2}$ on $x/R=0,0.25,\dots,3$; peak $0.385$ at $x/R=0.707$; the line [0, 0] is the axis.
figures.read: The axial field is zero at the centre, peaks at x/R=1/√2, then falls toward the point-charge 1/x² limit.

figures.title: The Gaussian-surface protocol
figures.why: the law is one line; every mistake is in the choice of surface, and the flow makes the choice mechanical.
figures.data: the four steps of §3.17 and the three admissible symmetries with their surfaces; the exit for "no symmetry".
figures.read: Match a spherical, cylindrical or planar Gaussian surface only when the source symmetry makes E constant on the relevant surface; otherwise the flow exits to direct methods.

figures.title: Field of a uniformly charged solid sphere
figures.why: the linear rise and the $1/r^2$ fall meeting at the surface is the profile the paper asks you to sketch, and the one students most often draw with a jump.
figures.data: $E/(kQ/R^2)$ against $r/R$ on $0,0.25,\dots,3$: $r/R$ inside, $(R/r)^2$ outside; the line [0, 0] is the axis.
figures.read: Inside the uniformly charged sphere E rises linearly from zero; outside it falls as 1/r², joining continuously at the surface.

figures.title: Field profile of a uniformly charged slab
figures.why: the linear interior and the flat exterior, joined without a jump, is the planar twin of F13.5 and a standard "sketch $E(x)$" item.
figures.data: $E/(\rho d/2\varepsilon_0)$ against $x/(d/2)$ on $-3,-2.5,\dots,3$: $x/(d/2)$ inside, $\pm1$ outside; the line [0, 0] is the axis.
figures.read: The slab field rises linearly through the material and becomes constant outside, with no jump at either face.

figures.title: Potential and field of a charged shell
figures.why: the pairing "V continuous, E jumps" at $r=R$ is the single most useful picture in the potential half of the chapter.
figures.data: on $r/R=0,0.25,\dots,3$: $V/(kQ/R)=1$ inside, $R/r$ outside; $E/(kQ/R^2)=0$ inside, $(R/r)^2$ outside; the line [0, 0] is the axis.
figures.read: The shell has constant potential and zero field inside; outside V falls as 1/r and E as 1/r². Potential is continuous at the surface while the field jumps.

figures.title: The correspondence chain of the standard fields
figures.why: the ledger has thirty rows but only four independent facts; seeing how each row collapses into the next is the fastest error detector on the paper.
figures.data: the limits of Part 3: rod → line ($L\to\infty$) → point ($d\gg L$); disc → sheet ($R\to\infty$) and → point ($x\gg R$); shell → point (outside) and → zero (inside); slab → sheet; dipole → two charges (near) and → $1/r^3$ (far); solid sphere → shell (charge pushed to the surface).
figures.read: Each finite-distribution result reduces to its simpler limit: line, sheet, point, shell, slab or dipole as the stated geometry changes.

figures.title: Triage for an electrostatics question
figures.why: the first thirty seconds decide whether the question takes two minutes or ten; the tree routes each opening line to its cheapest tool.
figures.data: the decision points of Part 4.1 and Part 7 T3, with the exits named by the block that owns them.
figures.read: Route discrete charges to superposition, symmetric continuous sources to Gauss, and general distributions to integration or potential.

figures.title: A ring's potential along its axis and across its plane
figures.why: the two curves are the saddle of (10.1) made visible — one bends down, the other up, from the same centre value.
figures.data: $V/(kQ/R)$ against distance from the centre in units of $R$, $0$ to $0.9$ in steps of $0.1$: along the axis $1/\sqrt{1+x^2}$; in the plane the exact ring potential $(2/\pi)K(m)/(1+\rho)$ with $m=4\rho/(1+\rho)^2$ and $K$ the complete elliptic integral of the first kind, evaluated by the arithmetic–geometric mean.
figures.read: Near the centre the in-plane potential curves upward while the axial potential curves downward; the opposite curvatures reveal a saddle.

drawings.title: Three charging mechanisms with electron transfer
drawings.show: three rows. Friction: a rod and a cloth before and after, with a handful of $e^-$ arrows crossing from cloth to rod and the final $+$/$-$ labels. Conduction: a charged sphere touching a neutral one, electrons flowing through the contact, both spheres ending with the same sign. Induction: a negative rod near a neutral sphere with $+$ on the near face and $-$ on the far face, then an earth wire draining the far-side electrons, then the wire removed, then the rod removed and the $+$ charge spreading over the sphere.
